title: Place Transition Words by Logic
description: Use transition-word punctuation and three-clause logic to decide whether a transition belongs before or after a full stop in SAT Boundaries questions.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first idea, even if you are unsure. You can continue without submitting an answer.

  1. ; consequently,
  2. , consequently;
  3. , consequently,
  4. ; consequently;

shared_prompt.title: Opening question
shared_prompt.html: The river flooded the lower trail. Park officials closed that route ___ the upper trail remained open throughout the week. Which choice best fits the logic?

blocks.html:
Two legal positions can say different things

The flood question asks where “consequently” belongs. Punctuation tells you which clause contains it; meaning tells you whether that connection makes sense.

We’ll start with a simpler contrast, then return to the trail.

shared_prompt.title: Two pollen samples
shared_prompt.html:
Version 1: The first soil sample contained pollen. The second sample, however, contained no pollen.

Version 2: The first soil sample contained pollen. The second sample contained no pollen, however.

blocks.html:
Follow “however” as it moves

Compare the two pollen sentences. Which facts contrast? Notice that moving the word within the same clause keeps that connection.

content.prompt: In both sample sentences, which two ideas does however contrast?
choices: the pollen in the samples and the soil around them
the second sample and the specific word pollen inside it
the first sample contained pollen and the second sample contained no pollen
the placement of the first period and the placement of the second one
content.hint: Temporarily move however to the beginning of the second sentence: 'However, the second sample contained no pollen.'
content.explanation: However marks a contrast between the complete idea before it and the complete idea in the clause that contains it. Moving the word within the second clause does not change that relationship.

blocks.html:
Connect complete ideas

A transition shows how one idea relates to another. “However” marks a contrast; “therefore” marks a result. An independent clause has a subject, a verb, and a complete thought, so it can stand as a sentence.

content.prompt: What is the main job of however in this passage? The first trial succeeded. The second trial, however, failed.
choices: It shows that the second trial contrasts with the first trial.
It turns the second trial into a question.
It makes the first clause dependent on the second.
It replaces the verb in the second clause.
content.hint: Read the two results: succeeded and failed. What relationship do they have?
content.explanation: However tells you that the current clause's failure contrasts with the previous clause's success.

blocks.html:
The clause works without the signpost

“The second trial, however, failed” remains complete when you remove “however.” Punctuation sets the transition apart: “However, the trial failed”; “The trial, however, failed”; “The trial failed, however.”

content.prompt: Which test shows that nevertheless is nonessential in this sentence? The sensor, nevertheless, recorded the change.
choices: Move the sensor to the very end of the sentence and reread the whole thing.
Replace recorded with a different verb and check whether the meaning changes.
Add a second subject directly after nevertheless and reread the sentence.
Remove nevertheless and its commas; 'The sensor recorded the change' remains complete.
content.hint: Nonessential information can be removed without destroying the sentence's grammatical core.
content.explanation: Removing the transition leaves a complete independent clause, so the transition is nonessential and must be offset by punctuation.

blocks.html:
The end is a possible position too

A transition can begin, interrupt, or end its clause. “The backup system worked, however” is a complete sentence. The word still connects the backup’s success with the preceding idea.

content.prompt: Which statement about transition placement is accurate?
choices: A transition must begin its independent clause.
A transition may begin, interrupt, or end its independent clause.
A transition at the end points forward to the next clause.
A transition becomes essential when it appears in the middle.
content.hint: Recall the three grammatical versions of 'the backup system worked.'
content.explanation: A transition can occur anywhere in its clause, including at the very end.

blocks.html:
Look backward from the clause containing it

“The forecast predicted clear skies. A storm arrived, however.” The contrast is between the forecast and the storm. “However” belongs to the storm clause even though it appears at the end.

content.prompt: In 'The forecast predicted clear skies. A storm arrived, however,' what does however connect?
choices: It connects storm forward to an idea that has to appear in the next sentence.
It connects the word clear to the word skies inside the first clause.
It connects 'A storm arrived' backward to 'The forecast predicted clear skies.'
It connects nothing but the two subjects, forecast and storm.
content.hint: Identify the complete clause that contains however, then look one independent clause backward.
content.explanation: Sentence-final however still belongs to the storm clause and points backward to the forecast clause.

blocks.html:
Now compare three clauses

Call the clauses A, B, and C. In “A. B, however; C,” the transition belongs to B. In “A. B; however, C,” it belongs to C. Both patterns can be grammatical, so meaning must decide.

Identify the pair it connects

If the transition belongs to B, test the connection from A to B. If it belongs to C, test B to C. A semicolon and a period both separate complete clauses for this decision.

content.prompt: If a choice creates 'A. B, therefore; C,' which relationship must therefore describe?
choices: C must be a result of A.
B must be a result of A.
C must be a result of B.
A must be a result of C.
content.hint: Therefore appears before the semicolon, at the end of B. Move it to the beginning of B.
content.explanation: Read it mentally as 'A. Therefore, B. C.' Therefore belongs to B and marks B as a result of A.

blocks.html:
Use A–B–C

  1. Find the three complete clauses.
  2. Use punctuation to place the transition in B or C.
  3. If helpful, move it to the start of that same clause in your mind.
  4. Test its meaning against the preceding clause.

shared_prompt.title: Backup telescope passage
shared_prompt.html: A: The observatory's main telescope was under repair. B: Astronomers used a smaller backup telescope ___ C: The backup instrument had been installed in 2018.

blocks.html:
Find the result in this passage

The repair explains why astronomers used the backup: A leads to B. Using the backup does not explain its installation date. “Therefore” belongs to B, before the full stop separating B and C.

content.prompt: Where must therefore go in the observatory passage?
choices: After the semicolon, because C is a result of B
After the semicolon, because A is a result of C
Before the semicolon, because C is a result of A
Before the semicolon, because B is a result of A
content.hint: Ask which event is the result of the telescope being under repair.
content.explanation: B is a result of A, so therefore belongs to B and must appear before the full stop between B and C.

blocks.html:
Hear the same connection another way

Think: “The main telescope was under repair. Therefore, astronomers used a backup. The backup had been installed in 2018.” Moving “therefore” to the end of the backup clause keeps that meaning.

content.prompt: The museum's climate-control system failed. Staff moved the paintings to a protected storage room ___ the room was renovated in 2022. Which choice fits the logic?
choices: , consequently;
; consequently,
, consequently,
; consequently;
content.solution:
Label the clauses: A is "The museum's climate-control system failed," B is "Staff moved the paintings to a protected storage room," and C is "the room was renovated in 2022."
Test the logic to find the result pair: the system failure caused the move, so B is a result of A; moving the paintings did not cause the 2022 renovation, so C is not a result of B.
Attach: consequently connects A to B, so it belongs at the end of B, before the full stop, which is ", consequently;". Placing it after the semicolon would attach it to C and wrongly test B to C.
Verify with the mental rewrite: "The museum's climate-control system failed. Consequently, staff moved the paintings to a protected storage room. The room was renovated in 2022."
So the answer is choice A, ", consequently;".
content.hint: Label the clauses A, B, and C. The system failure caused which clause: B or C?
content.explanation: A caused B, so consequently belongs at the end of B, before the semicolon. Moving it gives: 'The system failed. Consequently, staff moved the paintings.'

shared_prompt.title: Telescope repairs passage
shared_prompt.html: A: Repairs to the telescope ended on Monday. B: Astronomers expected to resume observations that night ___ C: Dense clouds covered the sky.

blocks.html:
This time the contrast comes later

In the new passage, the repairs explain the expectation of observing. The clouds contrast with that expectation. “However” belongs to C, after the full stop separating B and C.

content.prompt: Which choice fits the logic of the telescope repairs passage?
choices: , however;
, however,
; however,
; however;
content.solution:
Label the clauses: A is "Repairs to the telescope ended on Monday," B is "Astronomers expected to resume observations that night," and C is "dense clouds covered the sky."
Test the logic: A leads naturally to B, since finished repairs explain the expectation, so there is no contrast between A and B; the contrast is between B and C, because the astronomers expected to observe but clouds blocked the sky.
Attach: however connects B to C, so it belongs at the beginning of C, after the full stop; the semicolon ends B and "however," begins C.
Verify: "Astronomers expected to resume observations that night; however, dense clouds covered the sky" states the contrast between the right pair.
So the answer is choice C, "; however,".
content.hint: The contrast is between the expectation in B and the clouds in C. Attach however to the clause about the clouds.
content.explanation: The semicolon ends B, and 'however,' begins C. The transition points backward from C to the contrasting expectation in B.

blocks.html:
A period gives the same choice

“B, however. C” places the transition in B. “B. However, C” places it in C. Use the same A–B or B–C meaning test that you used with a semicolon.

content.prompt: The archive lost power. Staff carried the manuscripts to a secure room ___ room had opened five years earlier. Which period choice expresses the correct cause-and-result relationship?
choices: . Consequently, the
, consequently. The
, consequently, the
; consequently; the
content.hint: The power loss caused staff to carry the manuscripts. It did not cause the room to open years earlier. Put consequently in B, before the period.
content.explanation: Consequently belongs to B because B results from A: 'The archive lost power. Consequently, staff carried the manuscripts.' The transition can sit at the end of B before the period.

blocks.html:
Keep the word inside its own clause

To clarify “A. B, nevertheless; C,” think “A. Nevertheless, B. C.” This mental move helps you hear the connection. Keep the transition in B when you move it.

content.prompt: Which mental rewrite correctly clarifies 'A. B, nevertheless; C'?
choices: Nevertheless, A. B. C.
A. B. Nevertheless, C.
A. B; C, nevertheless.
A. Nevertheless, B. C.
content.hint: Nevertheless appears inside B before the full stop. Move it to the beginning of B, not into A or C.
content.explanation: The mental rewrite keeps nevertheless in B: 'A. Nevertheless, B. C.' Now it is easier to test the A–B contrast.

blocks.html:
“Though” needs one extra check

In “The match continued, though,” the word is a transition meaning “however.” In “Though the forecast predicted rain, the match continued,” it starts a dependent clause: a thought that needs a main clause to finish the sentence.

content.prompt: In which choice does though act as a nonessential transition meaning however?
choices: The match continued, though.
Though the match continued.
Though the match continued, the rain intensified.
The match that continued though the rain.
content.hint: Look for a complete independent clause that remains complete when though is removed.
content.explanation: Remove ', though' and 'The match continued' remains complete. Here though is a nonessential transition pointing backward.

blocks.html:
Check “though” at the front

“Though, the crews kept working” does not work like “However, the crews kept working.” Without that comma, “though the crews kept working” needs a main clause in the same sentence. It cannot stand alone after a period or semicolon.

choices: The forecast called for rain. Though, the crews kept working.
The forecast called for rain; though the crews kept working.
The forecast called for rain. The crews, though, kept working.
The forecast called for rain. Though the crews kept working.
content.hint: As a transition, though never leads its clause. When though is first, it is the subordinating word — then check what that does to the sentence.
content.explanation: Mid-clause with commas, though is a valid transition. The first version treats though like However, — a position it cannot take. The second puts a dependent clause after a semicolon, and the fourth leaves a dependent clause standing alone as a fragment.

blocks.html:
A semicolon needs two complete clauses

“The field, though, remained wet” can stand alone. “Though the field remained wet” cannot. Check the position and punctuation of “though” before treating it as a transition.

content.prompt: Why is the punctuation invalid in 'The organizers kept the outdoor venue; though the field remained wet'?
choices: A semicolon is not permitted to appear anywhere near the subordinating word though, whatever the clauses say.
The clause before the semicolon is missing its main verb, so it cannot stand alone.
Without a comma after though, 'though the field remained wet' is dependent, so it cannot stand after a semicolon.
The word though points forward here, attaching the wet field to a following sentence that does not exist.
content.hint: Read only the words after the semicolon. Can 'Though the field remained wet' stand alone?
content.explanation: Here though is a subordinating word, not a nonessential transition. It creates a dependent clause after a punctuation mark that requires an independent clause.

blocks.html:
Return to the flooded trail

Try the first question again. Identify the complete clauses, then put the transition with the pair of ideas it connects.

content.prompt: Return to the opening question. What answer do you get now?
choices: ; consequently,
, consequently;
, consequently,
; consequently;
content.hint: Decide which idea is a consequence of the flood. Keep consequently inside the clause expressing that result.
content.explanation: Consequently belongs to B because B results from A: 'The river flooded the lower trail. Consequently, park officials closed that route.' The sentence-final transition comes before the semicolon.
content.solution: Consequently belongs to B because B results from A: 'The river flooded the lower trail. Consequently, park officials closed that route.' The sentence-final transition comes before the semicolon.

content.prompt: Two choices, both grammatical: the transition before the period in one, after it in the other. From memory, what's the process that decides between them?
choices: Label A–B–C; attach the transition to B or C; move an end transition within its clause if helpful; test A–B or B–C logic; check whether though is truly a transition.
Label A–B–C; attach the transition to A or B; move an end transition into the next clause; test A–C logic; check whether though is truly a transition.
Label A–B–C; test A–B or B–C logic before attaching the transition; leave an end transition where it stands; treat though as a transition whenever it starts a clause.
Attach the transition to whichever clause is longest; label A–B–C afterward to confirm; test both A–B and B–C and keep whichever choice fits either.
content.explanation: You have it. Before the full stop means test A–B; after the full stop means test B–C. A transition may end its clause, and though without the transition comma may create a dependent clause instead.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: The new battery passed every laboratory test. Engineers expected it to last ten hours in the field ___ it stopped working after only six hours. Which choice best fits the logic?
choices: , however;
, however,
; however;
; however,
content.explanation: However begins C after the semicolon and points backward to the contrasting expectation in B.

content.prompt: City records from 1998 describe the harborfront mural as the largest and most expensive public artwork ever commissioned by the town council. The mural was expected to take a single summer to ______ delays in sourcing weather-resistant pigments stretched the project across three years. Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: complete, however,
complete. However,
complete however,
complete, however
content.explanation: "The mural was expected… to complete" and "delays… stretched the project" are both independent clauses, so "However" needs a full stop before it and a comma after. A comma before "however" splices the sentences no matter what follows it.

content.html:
Place the transition with its idea

When both positions are grammatical, let the relationship decide.
